body: Spam copy of https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/4857.
Oh, I'm so sorry, this is an attempted continuation.
Yes, that's right.

Thanks, @howard-e! I've pushed commit to remove the algo that was moved to CSS UI, and change "can be a button" to be closer to the proposed prose in https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/3526#issuecomment-689146382 (under "HTML"). The remaining "can be ..." needs this treatment as well.
This PR should now be ready for editorial review. It uses terms defined in https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537

> Although this PR does define the "can be" algorithms, I'll note that it doesn't accomplish the goal stated in the title, of defining how some properties disable appearance, because it doesn't finish the integration with CSS UI by mapping the computed (used?) value of "kind of widget" to actual appearances.

That is now part of CSS UI, see
https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537/files#diff-cc2f666bf7d93dcefcc3fffc4761793a54fba00c03b53b9dbdf81f5056f0b56eR2224

I guess the title here should be clarified. (Edit: fixed.)
Everything we identified in the test plan to test is now tested, see OP for links. Implementation bugs are filed. Getting there!

> That is now part of CSS UI, see
https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537/files#diff-cc2f666bf7d93dcefcc3fffc4761793a54fba00c03b53b9dbdf81f5056f0b56eR2224

Sure, but this PR doesn't explain when something is actually a (e.g.) button widget, because of the XXX boxes. So that section of CSS UI tells us that sometimes some properties cause a "none" appearance, but nothing tells us the difference between "none" appearance and "button" appearance.

Ah, yeah. Indeed, it needs to be defined. IIRC the UA styles aren't identical between browsers (or even same browser, across OSes), so it's not necessarily very simple. That's not to say that we shouldn't spec it, just that I prefer to deal with them as follow-ups so we can review and get sign off for each widget.

Rebased to resolve conflicts.

@domenic are you OK with landing this, and leave #7050 for follow-ups? We hope to land this next week so it can be [considered for Interop 2022](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/interop-2022/issues/11#issuecomment-966632869). @josepharhar is currently reviewing [these tests](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/30267).

Can you help by briefly summarizing what the normative consequences of (a strict reading of) this spec change are, given the XXX boxes leaving some stuff undefined? That would probably also help with the commit message.

Sure. The assumption is that the different kinds of widgets have different rendering from each other, and different from the `appearance: none` style.

The main consequence as compared to legacy browser implementations is that only the "appropriate" element can render as a particular widget kind. For example, only `<input type=checkbox>` can be a checkbox, not any element.

The other part is the addition of `appearance: auto` in the UA stylesheet, which is [observable](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/18591) with `getComputedStyle`.
@domenic they are introduced in https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537 in tandem with this PR

OK, I think I see now. However I'm still not sure this PR has any normative consequences, apart from the UA stylesheet changes and some improvements to the definition of meter.

From my read, this PR ensures that the "kind of widget" algorithm introduced in https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537 returns the correct value, based on various inputs. (The computed 'appearance' property; other author props; and the various "can be an X" algorithms defined here.) However, I can't find anything in the spec ecosystem which cares about the kind of widget. The only reference is a bunch of XXX boxes here, plus the one non-XXX definition for meter.

So I think the only normative, testable impacts of this PR are:

- It makes it clear that only sometimes are `meter` elements supposed to render as inline-block 1em by 5em boxes. It is very nice and precise about when that occurs. (Although, it does not tell us what should happen in the other case... so in theory the other case could _also_ be an inline-block 1em by 5em box, so I'm not sure we could even write tests for this.)
- It changes the UA stylesheet for various widgets to have `appearance: auto`.

But I think those normative impacts could be accomplished with much less text. In particular all of the "can be an X" algorithms, besides the one for meter, do nothing; they are just "dead code", since nothing in the spec ecosystem acts on any "kind of widget" besides meter.

So I still think it's not very valuable to merge this PR without working on https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7050. I think it gives a false sense of progress. If we are in a hurry to merge something now, then we should cut down this PR to only contain definitions for meter and the UA stylesheet changes, so that it does not contain so much misleading spec text that doesn't do anything currently.

Please let me know if I'm missing something and there is some other caller of "kind of widget" besides the XXX boxes and the meter definition. That would definitely change the story.

Your reading is correct, the last bit of the expected rendering for each kind of widget is not yet defined.

I don't agree that it means that the work done so far to pin down how the 'appearance' property works, most of which is https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537 , is effectively useless. It helped get interop between chromium and gecko which have already implemented this stuff, c.f.

https://chromestatus.com/feature/5070237827334144
https://chromestatus.com/feature/4867142128238592
https://chromestatus.com/feature/5913213940006912
https://chromestatus.com/feature/4715298156445696

WebKit has now also unprefixed, but still allows a `div` to render as a `button` with `-webkit-appearance: button`, which is in fact **not** conforming to this spec change -- a `div` must always have the "none" appearance. (Edit: my Safari TP might be outdated, so I'm not 100% sure about this -- upgrading now. Edit2: Confirmed with v135 on macOS Monterey.)

The "hurry" here is with Interop 2022, so that we can nudge WebKit to fix this aspect next year, and get better interop across all 3 engines.

Focusing on `meter` only through the lens of end-to-end testable requirements is not helping with anything IMO.

We can say that the rendering of the different kinds of widgets are UA defined, except that they must be different from one another. Would that help?

I'm sorry, I don't think that would help. It would just provide a wide swathe of implementation-defined behavior, which is discouraged in our working mode.

Ultimately, what is being proposed here is not a specification anyone could read in order to implement something interoperable or web-compatible. It's a bunch of algorithms that boil down to providing a very clear way of determining "type of widget", which is not used in the spec ecosystem (apart from meter).

To be clear, I don't think this work is useless. I think it's just half the story. (Or maybe more like 80% of it.) Unfortunately it's the sort of work where if you tell someone to implement half of a feature, that half doesn't compile. Instead of the sort where you tell someone to implement half of a feature, and there's half of the functionality available.

I don't know how the Interop2022 project's policies work, but perhaps an alternate route to pursue would be to not make them dependent on specs---since we don't have a spec for these features until that last half is done.

> WebKit has now also unprefixed, but still allows a div to render as a button with -webkit-appearance: button, which is in fact not conforming to this spec change -- a div must always have the "none" appearance.

It is conforming to this spec change, because nothing in this spec change says what being a button kind-of-widget vs. a none kind-of-widget means.

> It is conforming to this spec change, because nothing in this spec change says what being a button kind-of-widget vs. a none kind-of-widget means.

Hmm yeah, that's not good. I've tried to address this in https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537 now, so that there is a "should" requirement for every kind of widget:

https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537/files#diff-cc2f666bf7d93dcefcc3fffc4761793a54fba00c03b53b9dbdf81f5056f0b56eR2118

> I don't know how the Interop2022 project's policies work, but perhaps an alternate route to pursue would be to not make them dependent on specs---since we don't have a spec for these features until that last half is done.

The process and policies are a work in progress, but we've been looking for specs and tests for all proposals. However, we do have some flexibility in that we hand pick which tests to include. That means that if a spec has missing parts or things that nobody can commit to implementing yet, we can carefully avoid including tests for those aspects.

Concretely, assuming the spec(s) are in good shape, we could focus on `appearance: none`, but avoid testing `appearance: textarea`, even the pure "compute role" part of it.

Is `appearance: none` well defined at this point?

This PR + https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/6537 define the "compute the kind of widget" part for appearance. What is not yet well defined is the exact expected rendering for any kind of widget -- other than "none" meaning "must not use native appearance".

Sorry for the long pause.

The new additions seem helpful, and IMO start to tip this toward being useful to implementers. In particular, it seems if we assume "everybody knows" what "a native appearance of button" or "no native appearance" means, then the spec could be implemented end-to-end. I think we've merged things in the past where the boundaries of the feature rely on such ill-defined concepts, e.g. anything that relies on hit-testing.

My remaining worries are about the testability of the current setup, where it's not great to rely on such "everybody knows" knowledge:

- All requirements are "should" requirements, so any tests written would have to be `.optional` tests. Is that really where we want to end up, long term?
- There are no requirements that the native appearances be different from each other, or different from no native appearance. Until we have such requirements, it seems like Safari's implementation would still be conformant to the spec, despite failing the reference tests in https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/30267, since it's possible that the native appearance of button has the same rendering as no native appearance. We could assume such requirements, but I think it'd be best to name the tests as `.tentative` until such requirements are specified somewhere.

> The new additions seem helpful, and IMO start to tip this toward being useful to implementers.

Thanks.

> In particular, it seems if we assume "everybody knows" what "a native appearance of button" or "no native appearance" means, then the spec could be implemented end-to-end. I think we've merged things in the past where the boundaries of the feature rely on such ill-defined concepts, e.g. anything that relies on hit-testing.
> 
> My remaining worries are about the testability of the current setup, where it's not great to rely on such "everybody knows" knowledge:
> 
> * All requirements are "should" requirements, so any tests written would have to be `.optional` tests. Is that really where we want to end up, long term?

No, if/when we get consensus on the rendering for a kind of widget and it's well-defined, it can become a "must" requirement. The "none" kind of widget is "must" already.

> * There are no requirements that the native appearances be different from each other, or different from no native appearance. Until we have such requirements, it seems like Safari's implementation would still be conformant to the spec, despite failing the reference tests in [HTML: Compute kind of widget web-platform-tests/wpt#30267](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/30267), since it's possible that the native appearance of button has the same rendering as no native appearance.

No, it's not conforming -- the spec says that `<div style="appearance: button">` and `<div style="appearance: none">` both should have the "none" kind of widget, and so, regardless of what is expected for any of the other kinds of widgets, these two must render the same. But WebKit renders them differently.

> We could assume such requirements, but I think it'd be best to name the tests as `.tentative` until such requirements are specified somewhere.

Tests marked as both optional and tentative sort of signals that the test should be ignored. I'm not sure that's useful.

CSS also leaves the precise rendering of other things vague, and it doesn't prevent us from specifying and testing the machinery of how the relevant properties are computed. For example, [border-style](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-backgrounds-3/#the-border-style), [text-decoration](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-text-decor/#text-decoration-property).

> No, if/when we get consensus on the rendering for a kind of widget and it's well-defined, it can become a "must" requirement. The "none" kind of widget is "must" already.

OK, great. So we can rename them all to `.optional` for now, and remove that suffix when we are able to convert these into musts?

> No, it's not conforming -- the spec says...

I see, that makes sense; thanks for walking me through it.

Are all of the tests of that type, i.e., "the spec says they both must have the same kind of widget, so we will compare them with reftests"? If so then I agree `.tentative` is not needed.

I guess there is an additional assumption here, that two things with the same kind of widget must render the same way, which isn't strictly defined. But it seems reasonable to assume, and doensn't need to push us into `.tentative` territory.

> > No, if/when we get consensus on the rendering for a kind of widget and it's well-defined, it can become a "must" requirement. The "none" kind of widget is "must" already.
> 
> OK, great. So we can rename them all to `.optional` for now, and remove that suffix when we are able to convert these into musts?

All kinds of widgets (except "none") can render as rainbows, and the tests would pass. All kinds of widgets can even render identical to "none" and the tests would pass I believe.

They are the same element with the same style (except `appearance`), everything else is identical where the tested CSS property is set -- UA style vs author style.

The tests can fail if a `<button style="appearance: auto">` renders differently from another `<button style="appearance: auto">`. Or if the browser has different rendering for different kinds of widgets, but the choice of kind of widget is wrong ([c.f. `select` in Gecko](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1730147)).

I still don't think they have to be `.optional`. Let me know if you're not convinced, and I'll make the change so we're not blocked on this.

> Are all of the tests of that type, i.e., "the spec says they both must have the same kind of widget, so we will compare them with reftests"? If so then I agree `.tentative` is not needed.

Yes.

> I guess there is an additional assumption here, that two things with the same kind of widget must render the same way, which isn't strictly defined. But it seems reasonable to assume, and doensn't need to push us into `.tentative` territory.

OK.

So, I think this is the particular failure case I'm worried about:

- The browser renders `<button style="appearance: auto;">` as a native widget button
- But, the browser renders `<button style="apperance: auto; color: black;">` as _not_ a native widget button.
- (and, these different renderings are detectable via reftest)

In this case the test will fail, if I read it correctly, because it expects that setting `color: black` will not change the rendering. (i.e., `color` is not in the `fallbackProps` list in the test).

However, this behavior is allowed by the spec, from what I can tell. Because being kind-of-widget = button only means that you _should_ have native appearance button. It doesn't mean that you *must* have native appearance button.

Is this correct?

That seems correct.

Maybe we can change those "should"s to "must"s, though.
